claim_checks.claim: `private` and `protected` are enforced only during type checking. Runtime lookups, and bracket notation even during type checking, still reach the member: it is "soft private".
claim_checks.page_says: private and protected are only enforced during type checking. ... private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking.
claim_checks.note: The handbook covers runtime lookups for private and protected, but bracket access during type checking (and the 'soft private' label) only for private. The protected part rests on probe-01 alone (exit 0, empty stdout, TypeScript 5.9.3), yet it is worded as a general rule with no version: wider scope than either source.

claim_checks.claim: `#` fields stay private after compilation and have no bracket-notation escape hatch: they are "hard private".
claim_checks.page_says: JavaScript’s private fields (#) remain private after compilation and do not provide the previously mentioned escape hatches like bracket notation access, making them hard private.

claim_checks.claim: When compiling to ES2021 or lower, TypeScript replaces `#` with `WeakMap`s. The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks will degrade performance.
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #. ... Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance.
claim_checks.note: The WeakMap part entails. The handbook says 'could affect'; the claim says 'will degrade', a modal raised to MUST level. The handbook's note is also about hard runtime privacy mechanisms in general (closures, WeakMaps, private fields), not specifically the downlevelled WeakMaps.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements are not properties. They cannot be enumerated, deleted, proxied, or reached through `Object` methods, and `structuredClone()` copies them like public fields.
claim_checks.page_says: For this reason, structuredClone() does not clone private elements
claim_checks.note: The first sentence and the enumerate/delete/proxy/Object-method list entail MDN ('they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method'). The structuredClone clause says the opposite of MDN. probe-02 is a valid test of this clause and its output also contradicts it: `#x in structuredClone(new A())` printed `false` on Node 24.22.1. The doc's own Probes caption ('a structuredClone() copy of a class instance has no # field') contradicts this line too.

claim_checks.claim: Reading a `#` field from an object whose class did not declare it throws a `TypeError`. `#x in obj` checks for it without throwing.
claim_checks.page_says: If you access a private element from an object that doesn't have the element, a TypeError is thrown ... it is possible to "stamp" private fields onto unrelated objects.
claim_checks.note: MDN's condition is 'an object that doesn't have the element'; the claim swaps in 'whose class did not declare it' (the wording of the engine's error message). MDN's own Stamper example reads a private field from a plain object whose class never declared it without throwing, so the claim's rule is wider than the page. The `in` part entails ('return true if the private field or method exists, and false otherwise').

claim_checks.claim: V8 9.4 moved class-field initialization, including private fields, onto its inline-cache fast path. Before that it went through slower runtime calls.
claim_checks.page_says: The first issue has been fixed in V8 v9.7 ... Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call for class field initializations.
claim_checks.note: The page gives v9.7, not 9.4 (the doc's own front matter also says V8 >= 9.7). The claim also drops the page's condition that the new IC is used only 'when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough'.

claim_checks.claim: An injected collaborator (port, clock, logger) | `private readonly x` constructor parameter | A `#` name cannot be a parameter property
claim_checks.page_says: That this is not possible is a bit surprising because it increases the friction of refactoring from a TypeScript-only concept to a native JavaScript feature
claim_checks.note: The issue thread (a 2020 feature request) says it is not possible, so the text is grounded, but the source is Rank 6 cited in a role 3 section: a KB-15 breach recorded under violations. The Rank 1 handbook supports the same point: parameter properties are created by prefixing with public, private, protected or readonly.

claim_checks.claim: Object wrapped in a `Proxy` (some mocking and reactivity libraries) | `#` access does not go through the proxy | Private elements cannot be proxied
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method.

claim_checks.claim: Target ES2021 or lower | `#` becomes `WeakMap` lookups | TypeScript downlevels it
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #.

claim_checks.claim: Working around it with `--experimental-transform-types` | Runs on Node 24.22 with an `ExperimentalWarning` (re-tested 2026-11-03); the flag is removed in Node 26.0.0 | So code meant to run unbuilt keeps injected collaborators as `readonly #field`s assigned in the constructor
claim_checks.note: The removal in 26.0.0 entails. 'Runs on Node 24.22 with an ExperimentalWarning' is not found in the saved page (searched 'ExperimentalWarning', 'warning', 'transform-types'); the saved page is the v26.13.1 documentation and the re-test is a local run with no probe cited.

claim_checks.claim: Type stripping itself | Stable (stability 2) since Node 24.12.0 and 25.2.0; no warning since 24.3.0; Node ignores `tsconfig.json` and needs `.ts` extensions in relative imports | Node only deletes types
claim_checks.page_says: v25.2.0, v24.12.0 | Type stripping is now stable. ... v24.3.0, v22.18.0 | Type stripping no longer emits an experimental warning. ... Node.js ignores tsconfig.json files
claim_checks.note: Extensions: 'file extensions are mandatory in import statements and import() expressions: import './file.ts''. Stripping only: 'Node.js is only removing inline types'.

claim_checks.claim: In Node 24.22.1, `Object.getOwnPropertyNames()` never lists a `#` field
claim_checks.note: The probe cannot fail: its only check (`names.length > 5`) does not look for `#x` at all, the throw sits inside a `try { } catch {}` that swallows it, and `console.log('not listed')` runs unconditionally after the block. The harness 'pass' therefore backs nothing. MDN [^2] ('interacted with using any Object method') could support the claim if cited.

conflicts.winner: [^2] rank 3 (MDN: structuredClone() does not clone private elements), observed by [^probe-02] on Node 24.22.1
conflicts.loser: the doc's own statement, no source (How it works item 4: 'structuredClone() copies them like public fields'); the doc's Probes caption states the opposite

violations.evidence: C3: 'will degrade performance' where the handbook [^1] says the runtime privacy checks 'could affect performance' (modal raised to MUST level); the note is about runtime privacy mechanisms in general, not the WeakMap downlevel.
C4: 'structuredClone() copies them like public fields' is contradicted by MDN [^2] ('structuredClone() does not clone private elements') and by the cited probe-02, which printed false.
C6: 'V8 9.4' where the V8 blog [^3] says the fix shipped in V8 v9.7; the IC fast path also applies only when the initialization pattern is predictable enough.
C12: probe-03 swallows its own error in an empty catch, never checks for #x, and prints 'not listed' unconditionally, so it is an invalid probe.
The 'Where each form fits' table row 'A # name cannot be a parameter property' cites [^5], a Rank 6 GitHub issue, in a role 3 section (allowed ranks 1-4).

How it works item 4 states that structuredClone() copies private elements, while the higher-ranked MDN page [^2] and the doc's own Probes section (probe-02, role 4) say the clone has no # field; the Rank 3 position does not govern role 3 and the conflict is not arbitrated.

C1: bracket-notation access during type checking and the 'soft private' label are extended from private to protected; for protected only probe-01 (TypeScript 5.9.3) backs it, yet it is worded as a general rule with no version.

C5: 'from an object whose class did not declare it' replaces MDN's condition 'an object that doesn't have the element'; MDN's stamping example reads a private field from an unrelated object without a TypeError.
C10: 'Runs on Node 24.22 with an ExperimentalWarning' is not in the cited Node page [^4] (v26.13.1 docs) and no probe backs the local re-test.
[^6] (tc39/proposal-class-fields) is listed as backing How it works 2 but is never cited in the body.

The 'Where each form fits' table is a prescriptive choice guide, not mechanism; no section does the role 2 (concept architecture) or role 5 (reference and invariants) job; the Verification status line says 10 verified claims while the body carries 12 ✅ claims (15 marks).

'On a native ES2022+ target, reading and creating # fields costs the same as public fields' (and the Takeaways line 'measured cost is nil') generalizes one uncited local benchmark on Node 24.22 (V8 13.6) to every native ES2022+ target.

patch_instructions.action: Item 3: replace 'The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks will degrade performance.' with 'The handbook notes that runtime privacy checks (closures, WeakMaps or # fields) could affect performance.' ✅[^1]

Item 4: replace 'and `structuredClone()` copies them like public fields' with 'and `structuredClone()` does not clone them' ✅[^2]; keep ✅[^probe-02] worded as an observation ('in Node 24.22.1 the clone fails `#x in`').
Item 6: change 'V8 9.4' to 'V8 v9.7' and add the condition 'when V8 considers the initialization pattern predictable enough; otherwise it still falls back to a runtime call' ✅[^3].

Rewrite probe-03 so it can fail: drop the try/catch and the unconditional print, e.g. `const names = Object.getOwnPropertyNames(new (class { #x = 1; y = 2 })()); console.log(JSON.stringify(names));` with expect=stdout:["y"]; or cite MDN [^2] ('interacted with using any Object method') and remove ✅[^probe-03] until the probe is fixed.

'Where each form fits' row for injected collaborators: replace ✅[^5] with ✅[^1] (Parameter Properties: 'created by prefixing a constructor argument with one of the visibility modifiers public, private, protected, or readonly'), or move the claim to Edge cases (role 6), where a Rank 6 source is allowed.

Resolve the structuredClone conflict in favour of MDN [^2] (see the item 4 fix) so How it works and the probe-02 caption in Probes agree; if the old belief is worth keeping, record it in Edge cases as a misconception with [^2] as the refutation.

Item 1: keep 'bracket notation even during type checking' for `private` only ✅[^1], and add the protected case as an observation: 'In TypeScript 5.9.3, bracket access to a `protected` member also type-checks ✅[^probe-01]'.

Item 5: replace 'from an object whose class did not declare it' with 'from an object that does not have the element' ✅[^2], optionally noting MDN's stamping case (a base constructor that returns another object).
`--experimental-transform-types` row: keep ✅[^4] for 'removed in Node 26.0.0'; back 'Runs on Node 24.22 with an ExperimentalWarning' with a probe run on node:24.22.1 or mark it ⚠️.
Cite [^6] in the body where it applies (How it works item 2, its 'No backdoor to access private' section) or delete the entry.

Move the 'Where each form fits' table to a guidance section (for example under Trade-offs); add a short concept-architecture or reference section if the doc type expects one; update Verification status to the real count of ✅ claims after the fixes.

Qualify the performance sentence as measured: 'In one local benchmark on Node 24.22 (V8 13.6), reads and constructions of # fields cost the same as public fields', and link the benchmark artifact; apply the same wording to the Takeaways line.
